lesson.title: Ranks and Ropes: How Colonial Society Was Ordered
lesson.summary: Colonial American society was organized into a steep hierarchy of gentry, middling farmers and artisans, servants, and enslaved people, with race increasingly determining a person's legal status by the early 1700s.
lesson.body:
Colonial society was never a single, uniform thing. It was a patchwork of local hierarchies shaped by region, economy, and law, but across nearly every colony a similar basic structure took hold. At the top sat a small gentry class, wealthy landowners, successful merchants, and officeholders who dominated colonial governance, filling seats in bodies like Virginia's House of Burgesses or town governments in New England. Below them was a much larger middling sort, made up of independent farmers, skilled artisans, and small tradesmen who owned enough property to vote in most colonies but held little formal power. Further down were free laborers, tenant farmers, and indentured servants, and at the very bottom, with no legal standing as free people at all, were enslaved men and women.

Indentured servitude was, for much of the 1600s, the main way colonies filled their labor needs, especially in the Chesapeake. Poor English men and women signed contracts binding them to work for a master for a fixed term, usually four to seven years, in exchange for passage across the Atlantic. Servants occupied a harsh but temporary position: they could be bought, sold, and punished, yet they retained some legal protections and, in theory, gained freedom and sometimes land at the end of their term. That temporary status stood in sharp contrast to slavery in the colonies, where by law enslaved status was permanent and, increasingly, inherited through the mother regardless of the father's status.

The line between these two forms of unfree labor hardened after Bacon's Rebellion in 1676, when a mixed force of free and indentured colonists in Virginia, angry at the colonial government and at Native peoples on the frontier, briefly overturned the established order. Fearful of future alliances between poor whites and enslaved or servant workers of African descent, Virginia's colonial governance increasingly used law to separate the two groups, expanding slave codes and offering small privileges to poor whites that were denied to enslaved people. Over the following decades planters shifted decisively toward enslaved African labor, which was now a lifelong and inheritable status rather than a temporary contract, making it more economically permanent from a planter's point of view.

This structure varied by region even as its basic shape held. New England's economy of small farms, fishing, and shipbuilding produced a somewhat flatter society of independent farmers and merchants, with slavery present but not central to the economy. The Middle Colonies mixed prosperous farmers, craftsmen, and merchants in a more religiously and ethnically diverse population. The Southern colonies, built around plantation agriculture, developed the sharpest hierarchy, with a small planter elite controlling both land and enslaved labor.

Political power throughout the colonies was tied tightly to property ownership. Only free men who owned a certain amount of land or property could vote or hold office in most colonial governments, which meant that colonial governance itself reinforced the social hierarchy rather than challenging it. Women of all ranks had no independent political voice and, once married, saw their legal identity absorbed into their husband's under the English common law doctrine of coverture. This layered, unequal social order, resting on property, race, and gender, shaped colonial life long before anyone spoke of American independence, and its assumptions about who deserved a political voice would be tested, but not overturned, by the revolution to come.
